claim: UBIAD1 utilizes geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp) to synthesize the vitamin K2 subtype menaquinone-4.
source: UbiA prenyltransferase domain-containing protein-1 (UBIAD1) utilizes geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp) to synthesize the vitamin K2 subtype menaquinone-4.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Hirota et al., 2013; Nakagawa et al., 2010) in the introduction.

claim: UBIAD1 has emerged as a key regulator of sterol-accelerated, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD) of HMG CoA reductase.
source: The prenyltransferase has emerged as a key regulator of sterol-accelerated, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD) of HMG CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in synthesis of cholesterol and nonsterol isoprenoids including GGpp.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).

claim: Sterols induce binding of UBIAD1 to reductase, inhibiting its ERAD.
source: Sterols induce binding of UBIAD1 to reductase, inhibiting its ERAD.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Schumacher et al., 2015).

claim: Geranylgeraniol (GGOH) disrupts the binding between UBIAD1 and reductase.
source: Geranylgeraniol (GGOH), the alcohol derivative of GGpp, disrupts this binding and thereby stimulates ERAD of reductase and translocation of UBIAD1 to Golgi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).

claim: GGOH stimulates ERAD of reductase.
source: Geranylgeraniol (GGOH), the alcohol derivative of GGpp, disrupts this binding and thereby stimulates ERAD of reductase and translocation of UBIAD1 to Golgi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and Figure 3B.

claim: GGOH stimulates translocation of UBIAD1 to Golgi.
source: Geranylgeraniol (GGOH), the alcohol derivative of GGpp, disrupts this binding and thereby stimulates ERAD of reductase and translocation of UBIAD1 to Golgi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: Overexpression of Type 1 polyisoprenoid diphosphate phosphatase (PDP1) abolishes protein geranylgeranylation.
source: We now show that overexpression of Type 1 polyisoprenoid diphosphate phosphatase (PDP1), which dephosphorylates GGpp and other isoprenyl pyrophosphates to corresponding isoprenols, abolishes protein geranylgeranylation as well as GGOH-induced ERAD of reductase and Golgi transport of UBIAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1A showing that tetracycline-mediated induction of PDP1-Myc-FLAG abolished azido-geranylgeranylation.

claim: Overexpression of PDP1 abolishes GGOH-induced ERAD of reductase.
source: We now show that overexpression of Type 1 polyisoprenoid diphosphate phosphatase (PDP1), which dephosphorylates GGpp and other isoprenyl pyrophosphates to corresponding isoprenols, abolishes protein geranylgeranylation as well as GGOH-induced ERAD of reductase and Golgi transport of UBIAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing that GGOH-enhanced ERAD of reductase was blunted when overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG was induced.

claim: Overexpression of PDP1 abolishes GGOH-induced Golgi transport of UBIAD1.
source: We now show that overexpression of Type 1 polyisoprenoid diphosphate phosphatase (PDP1), which dephosphorylates GGpp and other isoprenyl pyrophosphates to corresponding isoprenols, abolishes protein geranylgeranylation as well as GGOH-induced ERAD of reductase and Golgi transport of UBIAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing that GGOH-induced translocation of UBIAD1 from ER to Golgi was impeded by tetracycline-induced overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG.

claim: GGOH-induced ERAD of reductase and Golgi transport of UBIAD1 are enhanced in the absence of PDP1.
source: Conversely, these reactions are enhanced in the absence of PDP1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing enhanced GGOH-induced ERAD of reductase in PDP1 knockdown cells.

claim: PDP1 dephosphorylates GGpp and other isoprenyl pyrophosphates to corresponding isoprenols.
source: We now show that overexpression of Type 1 polyisoprenoid diphosphate phosphatase (PDP1), which dephosphorylates GGpp and other isoprenyl pyrophosphates to corresponding isoprenols, abolishes protein geranylgeranylation as well as GGOH-induced ERAD of reductase and Golgi transport of UBIAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Fukunaga et al., 2006; Miriyala et al., 2010).

claim: PDP1-mediated hydrolysis of GGpp significantly contributes to a feedback mechanism that maintains optimal intracellular levels of the nonsterol isoprenoid.
source: Our findings indicate PDP1-mediated hydrolysis of GGpp significantly contributes to a feedback mechanism that maintains optimal intracellular levels of the nonsterol isoprenoid.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mevalonate is a crucial intermediate in a branched pathway that produces cholesterol and nonsterol isoprenoids.
source: Mevalonate is a crucial intermediate in a branched pathway that produces cholesterol and nonsterol isoprenoids such as farnesyl pyrophosphate (Fpp), geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp), ubiquinone-10, dolichol, heme, and the vitamin K2 subtype menaquinone-4 (MK-4).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).

claim: Cholesterol plays an essential role in maintenance of membrane structure.
source: These end products of mevalonate metabolism play essential roles in a variety of cellular processes ranging from the maintenance of membrane structure (cholesterol), protein prenylation (Fpp and GGpp) and asparagine-linked glycosylation (dolichol) to electron transport (ubiquinone-10 and heme) and γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in specific proteins (MK-4) (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).

claim: Fpp and GGpp play essential roles in protein prenylation.
source: These end products of mevalonate metabolism play essential roles in a variety of cellular processes ranging from the maintenance of membrane structure (cholesterol), protein prenylation (Fpp and GGpp) and asparagine-linked glycosylation (dolichol) to electron transport (ubiquinone-10 and heme) and γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in specific proteins (MK-4) (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).

claim: Dolichol plays an essential role in asparagine-linked glycosylation.
source: These end products of mevalonate metabolism play essential roles in a variety of cellular processes ranging from the maintenance of membrane structure (cholesterol), protein prenylation (Fpp and GGpp) and asparagine-linked glycosylation (dolichol) to electron transport (ubiquinone-10 and heme) and γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in specific proteins (MK-4) (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).

claim: Ubiquinone-10 and heme play essential roles in electron transport.
source: These end products of mevalonate metabolism play essential roles in a variety of cellular processes ranging from the maintenance of membrane structure (cholesterol), protein prenylation (Fpp and GGpp) and asparagine-linked glycosylation (dolichol) to electron transport (ubiquinone-10 and heme) and γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in specific proteins (MK-4) (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).

claim: MK-4 plays an essential role in γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in specific proteins.
source: These end products of mevalonate metabolism play essential roles in a variety of cellular processes ranging from the maintenance of membrane structure (cholesterol), protein prenylation (Fpp and GGpp) and asparagine-linked glycosylation (dolichol) to electron transport (ubiquinone-10 and heme) and γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in specific proteins (MK-4) (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).

claim: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in certain types of cancers.
source: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in numerous diseases including certain types of cancers, Alzheimer's disease, osteoporosis, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in numerous diseases including certain types of cancers, Alzheimer's disease, osteoporosis, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in osteoporosis.
source: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in numerous diseases including certain types of cancers, Alzheimer's disease, osteoporosis, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
source: Dysregulation of mevalonate metabolism has been implicated in numerous diseases including certain types of cancers, Alzheimer's disease, osteoporosis, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Fusaro et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2018; Mullen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: Inhibition of mevalonate synthesis appears to elicit immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory responses that influence infectious diseases caused by various pathogens.
source: Moreover, inhibition of mevalonate synthesis appears to elicit immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory responses that influence infectious diseases caused by various pathogens (viruses, protozoa, fungi, and bacteria) (Parihar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Parihar et al., 2019).

claim: Synthesis of mevalonate is catalyzed by the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG CoA) reductase.
source: Synthesis of mevalonate is catalyzed by the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG CoA) reductase, which is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through an N-terminal membrane domain that precedes a cytosolic catalytic domain (Liscum et al., 1985; Roitelman et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Liscum et al., 1985; Roitelman et al., 1992).

claim: HMG CoA reductase is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through an N-terminal membrane domain that precedes a cytosolic catalytic domain.
source: Synthesis of mevalonate is catalyzed by the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG CoA) reductase, which is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through an N-terminal membrane domain that precedes a cytosolic catalytic domain (Liscum et al., 1985; Roitelman et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Liscum et al., 1985; Roitelman et al., 1992).

claim: The reductase is targeted by a unique feedback regulatory system that operates through multiple mechanisms to ensure cells constantly produce nonsterol isoprenoids, but avoid overaccumulation of cholesterol and/or its sterol precursors.
source: The reductase is targeted by a unique feedback regulatory system that operates through multiple mechanisms to ensure cells constantly produce nonsterol isoprenoids, but avoid overaccumulation of cholesterol and/or its sterol precursors (Brown and Goldstein, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Brown and Goldstein, 1980).

claim: One feedback regulatory mechanism involves accelerated ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of reductase from membranes.
source: One of these mechanisms involves accelerated ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of reductase from membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Accumulation of certain sterols within membranes of the ER initiates ERAD of reductase by causing it to bind ER membrane proteins called Insig-1 and Insig-2.
source: Accumulation of certain sterols within membranes of the ER initiates ERAD of reductase by causing it to bind ER membrane proteins called Insig-1 and Insig-2 (Sever et al., 2003a; Sever et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Sever et al., 2003a; Sever et al., 2003b).

claim: Ubiquitination of reductase by Insig-associated ubiquitin ligases triggers its extraction across the ER membrane, followed by dislocation into the cytosol for degradation by 26 S proteasomes.
source: Subsequent ubiquitination of reductase by Insig-associated ubiquitin ligases triggers its extraction across the ER membrane, followed by dislocation into the cytosol for degradation by 26 S proteasomes (Elsabrouty et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2018; Jo et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2014; Song et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Elsabrouty et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2018; Jo et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2014; Song et al., 2005).

claim: Knock-in mice expressing endogenous reductase resistant to sterol-induced ubiquitination accumulate the protein in multiple tissues, despite reduced levels of its mRNA.
source: The physiological significance of sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase is highlighted by the finding that knock-in mice expressing endogenous reductase resistant to sterol-induced ubiquitination accumulate the protein in multiple tissues, despite reduced levels of its mRNA (Hwang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Hwang et al., 2016).

claim: Nonsterol, mevalonate-derived products augment the ERAD of reductase, but only in the presence of sterols.
source: Nonsterol, mevalonate-derived products augment the ERAD of reductase, but only in the presence of sterols (Correll and Edwards, 1994; Nakanishi et al., 1988; Roitelman and Simoni, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Correll and Edwards, 1994; Nakanishi et al., 1988; Roitelman and Simoni, 1992).

claim: The addition to cells of geranylgeraniol (GGOH), but not farnesol (FOH), reproduces the augmentation of sterol-accelerated reductase ERAD.
source: The addition to cells of geranylgeraniol (GGOH), but not farnesol (FOH), reproduces the augmentation of sterol-accelerated reductase ERAD (Sever et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Sever et al., 2003a). It is also supported by experimental data in Figure 5B.

claim: FOH and GGOH are alcohol derivatives of Fpp and GGpp, respectively.
source: FOH and GGOH are alcohol derivatives of Fpp and GGpp, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: GGOH synergizes with sterols to accelerate ERAD of reductase by enhancing extraction of the ubiquitinated enzyme across ER membranes.
source: Subsequent studies revealed that GGOH synergizes with sterols to accelerate ERAD of reductase by enhancing extraction of the ubiquitinated enzyme across ER membranes (Morris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Morris et al., 2014).

claim: UBIAD1 produces MK-4 by using GGpp to prenylate the naphthoquinone menadione (vitamin K3) that is derived from dietary phylloquinone (vitamin K1).
source: This new player, UbiA prenyltransferase domain-containing protein-1 (UBIAD1), produces MK-4 by using GGpp to prenylate the naphthoquinone menadione (vitamin K3) that is derived from dietary phylloquinone (vitamin K1) (Hirota et al., 2013; Nakagawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Hirota et al., 2013; Nakagawa et al., 2010).

claim: Sterols stimulate binding of UBIAD1 to a subset of reductase molecules, inhibiting a post-ubiquitination step in their ERAD.
source: Current evidence indicates that sterols also stimulate binding of UBIAD1 to a subset of reductase molecules, inhibiting a post-ubiquitination step in their ERAD (Schumacher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Schumacher et al., 2015).

claim: Inhibition of reductase ERAD permits continuous synthesis of mevalonate for incorporation into GGpp and other nonsterol isoprenoids, even when sterols are abundant.
source: Inhibition of reductase ERAD permits continuous synthesis of mevalonate for incorporation into GGpp and other nonsterol isoprenoids, even when sterols are abundant (Schumacher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Schumacher et al., 2018).

claim: The addition to cells of GGOH causes release of UBIAD1 from reductase.
source: The addition to cells of GGOH causes release of UBIAD1 from reductase; this release relieves inhibition of ERAD and triggers translocation of UBIAD1 from the ER to Golgi (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).

claim: Release of UBIAD1 from reductase relieves inhibition of ERAD.
source: The addition to cells of GGOH causes release of UBIAD1 from reductase; this release relieves inhibition of ERAD and triggers translocation of UBIAD1 from the ER to Golgi (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).

claim: Release of UBIAD1 from reductase triggers translocation of UBIAD1 from the ER to Golgi.
source: The addition to cells of GGOH causes release of UBIAD1 from reductase; this release relieves inhibition of ERAD and triggers translocation of UBIAD1 from the ER to Golgi (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).

claim: Missense mutations in the UBIAD1 gene cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD).
source: Missense mutations in the UBIAD1 gene cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD), an autosomal dominant eye disease in humans characterized by the corneal accumulation of cholesterol (Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).

claim: Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD) is an autosomal dominant eye disease in humans characterized by the corneal accumulation of cholesterol.
source: Missense mutations in the UBIAD1 gene cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD), an autosomal dominant eye disease in humans characterized by the corneal accumulation of cholesterol (Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).

claim: SCD-associated UBIAD1 resists GGOH-induced release from HMGCR.
source: SCD-associated UBIAD1 resists GGOH-induced release from HMGCR and is sequestered in membranes of the ER (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).

claim: SCD-associated UBIAD1 is sequestered in membranes of the ER.
source: SCD-associated UBIAD1 resists GGOH-induced release from HMGCR and is sequestered in membranes of the ER (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016).

claim: ERAD of reductase becomes inhibited by the ER sequestered, SCD-associated UBIAD1, which leads to enhanced synthesis and intracellular accumulation of cholesterol in both cultured cells and tissues of knock-in mice that express SCD-associated UBIAD1.
source: ERAD of reductase becomes inhibited by the ER sequestered, SCD-associated UBIAD1, which leads to enhanced synthesis and intracellular accumulation of cholesterol in both cultured cells and tissues of knock-in mice that express SCD-associated UBIAD1 (Jo et al., 2019; Schumacher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Jo et al., 2019; Schumacher et al., 2018).

claim: Metabolic labeling studies revealed that FOH and GGOH can become converted to their phosphorylated derivatives (Fpp and GGpp) and utilized for the synthesis of sterols and protein prenylation.
source: Metabolic labeling studies revealed that FOH and GGOH can become converted to their phosphorylated derivatives (Fpp and GGpp) and utilized for the synthesis of sterols and protein prenylation (Crick et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Crick et al., 1997).

claim: Kinases that phosphorylate isoprenols have been reported in plants and bacteria.
source: Kinases that phosphorylate these isoprenols have been reported in plants and bacteria (Ohnuma et al., 1996; Thai et al., 1999); however, mammalian counterparts of these enzyme remain to be identified and characterized.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Ohnuma et al., 1996; Thai et al., 1999).

claim: Mammalian counterparts of isoprenol kinases remain to be identified and characterized.
source: Kinases that phosphorylate these isoprenols have been reported in plants and bacteria (Ohnuma et al., 1996; Thai et al., 1999); however, mammalian counterparts of these enzyme remain to be identified and characterized.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Type 1 polyisoprenoid diphosphate phosphatase (PDP1) is an integral ER membrane protein with a cytosolic active site that preferentially hydrolyzes isoprenyl pyrophosphates such as Fpp and GGpp to generate FOH and GGOH, respectively.
source: Type 1 polyisoprenoid diphosphate phosphatase (PDP1) is an integral ER membrane protein with a cytosolic active site that preferentially hydrolyzes isoprenyl pyrophosphates such as Fpp and GGpp to generate FOH and GGOH, respectively (Fukunaga et al., 2006; Miriyala et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Fukunaga et al., 2006; Miriyala et al., 2010).

claim: Overexpression of PDP1 reduces intracellular levels of isoprenyl pyrophosphates and inhibits protein prenylation.
source: Overexpression of PDP1 reduces intracellular levels of isoprenyl pyrophosphates and inhibits protein prenylation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A showing that overexpression of PDP1 abolished protein azido-geranylgeranylation.

claim: Protein azido-geranylgeranylation was abolished by tetracycline-mediated induction of PDP1-Myc-FLAG.
source: Protein azido-geranylgeranylation was abolished by tetracycline-mediated induction of PDP1-Myc-FLAG (lanes e and f), suggesting the modification was inhibited by PDP1-catalyzed hydrolysis of azido-geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate as previously reported (Miriyala et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1A and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: GGOH enhanced ERAD of reductase, which was indicated by its disappearance from membranes.
source: The results show that GGOH enhanced ERAD of reductase, which was indicated by its disappearance from membranes (Figure 1B, compare lane a with lanes b-e).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1B and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: GGOH-enhanced ERAD of reductase was blunted when overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG was induced by tetracycline.
source: This GGOH-enhanced ERAD of reductase was blunted when overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG was induced by tetracycline (compare lane f with lanes g-j).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1B and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: Serine-212 of PDP1 lies within the phosphatase catalytic motif; its mutation to threonine (S212T) abolishes enzymatic activity.
source: Serine-212 of PDP1 lies within the phosphatase catalytic motif; its mutation to threonine (S212T) abolishes enzymatic activity (Miriyala et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation (Miriyala et al., 2010).

claim: GGOH enhanced the ERAD of the membrane domain of reductase.
source: As expected, GGOH enhanced the ERAD of the membrane domain of reductase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, lanes 1 and 2); this ERAD was enhanced upon co-expression of catalytically inactive PDP1 (S212T)-FLAG (lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: ERAD of the membrane domain of reductase was enhanced upon co-expression of catalytically inactive PDP1 (S212T)-FLAG.
source: As expected, GGOH enhanced the ERAD of the membrane domain of reductase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, lanes 1 and 2); this ERAD was enhanced upon co-expression of catalytically inactive PDP1 (S212T)-FLAG (lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: Treatment of cells with the oxysterol 25-hydroxycholesterol (25-HC) stimulated reductase ERAD.
source: Subsequent treatment of the cells with the oxysterol 25-hydroxycholesterol (25-HC) stimulated reductase ERAD as expected (Figure 1C, compare lanes a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1C and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: The oxysterol 25-HC blocked proteolytic activation of sterol regulatory binding-protein-2 (SREBP-2).
source: The oxysterol also blocked proteolytic activation of sterol regulatory binding-protein-2 (SREBP-2), which was indicated by the disappearance of proteolytically released fragments of SREBP-2 from nuclei and concurrent accumulation of its membrane-bound precursor (compare lanes a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1C and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: GGOH enhanced ERAD of reductase that was stimulated by 25-HC.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Sever et al., 2003a), GGOH enhanced ERAD of reductase that was stimulated by 25-HC (lanes d and e).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1C and is directly shown in the figure. It is also supported by a citation (Sever et al., 2003a).

claim: The oxysterol continued to accelerate reductase ERAD upon inducible overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG; however, the effect of GGOH on this ERAD was diminished.
source: The oxysterol continued to accelerate reductase ERAD upon inducible overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG; however, the effect of GGOH on this ERAD was diminished (compare lanes b-e with g-j).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1C and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: UBIAD1 exhibited a reticular localization indicative of the ER when cells were depleted of nonsterol isoprenoids through incubation in compactin.
source: As we previously established in several studies (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2018), UBIAD1 exhibited a reticular localization indicative of the ER when cells were depleted of nonsterol isoprenoids through incubation in compactin (Figure 2A, panel 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2A and is directly shown in the figure. It is also supported by citations (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2018).

claim: The addition to the cells of GGOH triggered the translocation of UBIAD1 from the ER to the Golgi.
source: The addition to the cells of GGOH triggered the translocation of UBIAD1 from the ER to the Golgi as expected (panels 2–4).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2A and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: GGOH-induced translocation of UBIAD1 from ER to Golgi was impeded by tetracycline, which induced overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG.
source: GGOH-induced translocation of UBIAD1 from ER to Golgi was impeded by tetracycline (compare panels 1–4 with 5–8), which induced overexpression of PDP1-Myc-FLAG (compare panels 9–12 with 13–16).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2A and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: In mock-transfected cells, UBIAD1-Myc localized to the Golgi of the isoprenoid-replete cells.
source: In mock-transfected cells, UBIAD1-Myc localized to the Golgi of the isoprenoid-replete cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel 1) and compactin caused the protein's relocalization to the ER (panel 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: Compactin caused UBIAD1-Myc's relocalization to the ER.
source: In mock-transfected cells, UBIAD1-Myc localized to the Golgi of the isoprenoid-replete cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel 1) and compactin caused the protein's relocalization to the ER (panel 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: In the absence of compactin, UBIAD1-Myc localized to the Golgi upon co-expression with PDP1 (S212T)-Myc.
source: In the absence of compactin, UBIAD1-Myc localized to the Golgi upon co-expression with PDP1 (S212T)-Myc (panel 3); however, the protein remained in the Golgi upon compactin-mediated depletion of nonsterol isoprenoids (panel 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: UBIAD1-Myc remained in the Golgi upon compactin-mediated depletion of nonsterol isoprenoids when co-expressed with PDP1 (S212T)-Myc.
source: In the absence of compactin, UBIAD1-Myc localized to the Golgi upon co-expression with PDP1 (S212T)-Myc (panel 3); however, the protein remained in the Golgi upon compactin-mediated depletion of nonsterol isoprenoids (panel 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is directly shown in the figure.

claim: Overexpression of PDP1 accelerates the hydrolysis of GGpp and thereby blunts ERAD of reductase and ER-to-Golgi transport of UBIAD1 stimulated by the addition to cells of GGOH.
source: Results of Figures 1 and 2A indicate that overexpression of PDP1 accelerates the hydrolysis of GGpp and thereby blunts ERAD of reductase and ER-to-Golgi transport of UBIAD1 stimulated by the addition to cells of GGOH.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figures 1 and 2A.

claim: Structural studies indicate some SCD-associated mutations in UBIAD1 reduce the enzyme's affinity for GGpp.
source: Structural studies indicate some SCD-associated mutations in UBIAD1 reduce the enzyme's affinity for GGpp (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).
